extracted.intended_audience: improv performers, troupe leaders, and producers (beginners and intermediates)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for performing improvised comedy in public and for starting, running, and producing an improv theatre company, covering stagecraft, team management, promotion, and technical logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality in scene choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Know why you do what you do in scenes, rather than following random rules and freewheeling while the audience giggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to make an intelligent argument to defend your choices; act with purpose rather than mere chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get onstage — perform publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: There must come a day when you perform in public for the first time; otherwise it's all foreplay and no orgasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't wait until you think you're 'ready'—readiness comes from doing gigs. If your teachers set up a first show, take it; invite friends to create a fuller, anonymous audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an audience of friends/family strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite friends and family to see your first show so you have a nice full house and familiar faces become anonymous in a crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full house reduces the pressure of being singled out and makes the experience less intimidating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start small and build experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can perform for ten or fifteen minutes and then leave the stage to a more experienced group, that's good — you don't have to wait months longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three months of work can be enough to hold a friendly audience; learning happens by performing repeatedly (first leads to hundredth, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe anxiety and embrace failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that performance fears are mostly about status loss and not physical harm; learn to 'fail and stay happy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training like 'I Suck And I Love To Fail' helps; if you screw up but remain happy, the audience often responds positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical arrival and warm-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Get to the venue promptly so you can acclimatize, warm up with fellow players, and avoid last-minute panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be organized, know the theatre location, and leave extra travel time for delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overplanning on performance day
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't give yourself too much free time fretting about the show; overplanning will get in your way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange distracting activities during the day so you can walk onstage and see what shows up rather than following a plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-goal-per-show rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Know your strengths and weaknesses and give yourself one thing—and only one thing—to work on during the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick an easily achievable aim (e.g., 'say yes to offers' or 'fail and stay happy') and check afterwards whether you met it; defer other critiques to future shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: No alcohol before performing
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't drink before the show; a pint to steady nerves will only dull your senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy yourself and be collegial
rubrics_metrics.description: Have fun; nobody has to perform improvised comedy and you're doing it by choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be good to work with—support your teammates onstage and offstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader's role in rallying the team
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're setting up a group, rally the troops before the show and look after them during the night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell them you love them, treat them as marvelous talents onstage, congratulate them after the show, and avoid heavy notes immediately after a first show—introduce notes gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-show space-check
rubrics_metrics.description: After the show, check out the space again and notice how familiar it feels—performing conquers the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a confidence-building exercise for future shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start a show by treating it like hosting a party
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing a show is like throwing a party: choose venue, invite people, arrange food/drink, design publicity, and be present to welcome attendees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break tasks into smaller jobs and delegate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance: democracy vs benign dictatorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to run the company as a democracy or a benign dictatorship; the authors recommend the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracy shares workload but can create politics; dictatorship gives control but invites complaints. Be prepared for tradeoffs and continual justification of decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy for no-shows and replacements
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a rule that people must find their own replacements if they can't do a job or drop out of a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure everyone has a full contact list so the burden doesn't fall on one organizer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start a company if you hate administration and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Running a company requires being thick-skinned and organized; many improvisers lack these traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you dislike criticism, complaining, or administrative work, reconsider starting a company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't try to please everyone—insist on quality
rubrics_metrics.description: You will be criticized; it's better to put on the show you want and insist on quality than to attempt to satisfy all tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider an outside director for objective notes; if none, take turns being the outside eye and use short, controlled notes sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a structured post-show notes process
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a note-taker to hold a five-minute notes session immediately after the show where they give their opinion without debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extended arguments about who blocked whom; move any longer discussion to the bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting carefully and testing chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting is tricky—try people a couple of times before deciding and drop those you don't enjoy playing with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for performers who love improv and with whom you have chemistry; be prepared to invite new people to refresh the ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional boundaries within the company
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid turning your company into a social club where people can't give each other notes or can't be parted from the group when not working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find a balance between friendship and the ability to give/receive constructive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a show format that fits your strengths and has a clear hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide 'what show' you will do—pick formats that play to your team's strengths and make a clear promise to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider formats like Gorilla Theatre, TellTales, Theatresports, DreamDate, etc., and weigh how easy each is to sell and execute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick a name thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose show and group names that describe what the audience will see but avoid overly narrow or pun-heavy names that pigeonhole you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Google potential names to check availability and consider long-term implications for bookings (e.g., children's parties vs comedy clubs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide show frequency based on capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how often to stage shows—weekly, fortnightly, monthly, or runs—balancing workload, rehearsal time, and audience building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New companies may prefer monthly shows; runs (performing nightly for several weeks) offer focused practice and marketing windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal space — pay for a proper space
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a cheap rehearsal space rather than using someone's living room, which can be distracting and unprofessional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember workshop venues may be covered by fees, but show rehearsals typically come out of show takings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue choice: cabaret vs theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to do a cabaret (tables) or theatre (rows); theatres are easier to play because audience attention is focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore options like rooms above pubs (flexible timing) or late night slots in established theatres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about performing in stand-up clubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing short improv sets in stand-up clubs can be daunting due to different audience expectations and energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If attempting it, seek friendly clubs or negotiate a regular slot; consider mic/technical constraints that limit physicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design effective fliers and posters
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in a good photograph and well-designed fliers; include a map and all key information (booking, price, start time) and proofread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid silly costumes in photos unless central to the show's idea; distribute widely (shops, shows, workshops) and have team members carry fliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an up-to-date website and mailing list
rubrics_metrics.description: Register a short domain name, keep the site current with performance details, and provide mailing-list sign-up on every page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use link exchanges to boost search ranking and leverage social networks and discussion boards to promote the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue press and listings proactively
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit to listings (e.g., PA Listings) well in advance (six to eight weeks) and pursue reviews and editorial coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal-themed shows can attract picture editors; keep press clippings for quotes and legitimacy, and send short, well-laid-out press releases highlighting what's different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide advance ticketing and box-office procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow advance booking and payment (even if it costs a percentage), and check theatre box-office capabilities; have a staffed cash box for venues without one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ticketing services if needed; count cash at start and end of night and record tickets available/sold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage opening tone — avoid over-polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overproduced openings (pumping rock music and laser displays) which reduce room for risk; slickness can make work formulaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A charismatic host who creates a friendly mood can help, but don't let them dominate; explain format quickly and only what's necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage performers to interact 'as themselves'
rubrics_metrics.description: Have as many team members as possible interact with the audience as themselves so they can take over hosting duties if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theatrical formats a host may be unnecessary—always ask what the show actually needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music choices and technical coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide between live musicians or recorded music; recorded music offers breadth but requires performers to fit actions to the tracks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern setups (laptops/iPods) give access to many tracks; lighting and sound operators must be bold and responsive—preferably improvisers who understand timing and endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lighting and music to signal scene endings
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest way for a scene to end is for the lights to come down, ideally with a burst of music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lighting improviser has power to create endings; players and directors can also signal scene ends (e.g., calling 'scene', stage slap), but coordinate to avoid clumsy endings; pace problems can often be traced to the tech booth.
